query: Earlier studies established BCC refractory high-entropy alloys such as MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW with excellent high-temperature mechanical properties, while systems including AlNbTiV, NbHfTiV, and AlCrNbTiV also showed favorable mechanical behavior. NbZrTi-based alloys provide broad scope for regulating composition and properties, but changes in elemental identity and proportion can alter both phase constitution and mechanical performance. Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered BCC solid solution with a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa; however, its high Mo content increases the electronegativity difference and is associated with reduced plasticity. Given the constraint of preserving high strength while improving plasticity under room-temperature compression, what single intervention could overcome this limitation? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and its mechanism, predicts quantitative or directional changes relative to equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo, defines the conditions and limits of the effect, cites supporting evidence from the prior results summarized above, and proposes an experiment with explicit observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partial substitution of Mo with additional Nb (replacing approximately 10–30% of Mo) in the NbZrTiHfMo alloy will improve room-temperature plasticity by reducing electronegativity-induced brittleness while maintaining high compressive strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo disordered BCC solid solution where high Mo content leads to a high yield strength (~1719 MPa) but limited ductility due to strong Mo-induced lattice rigidity.
generation.intervention: Reduce the Mo content by substituting 10–30% of Mo with extra Nb, while keeping Zr, Ti, and Hf at equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios.
generation.conditions: Synthesize the modified alloys by arc melting or powder metallurgy under inert conditions; ensure the disordered BCC structure is preserved using XRD and SEM; test using room-temperature uniaxial compression.
generation.structural_mediator: Increasing Nb content modifies the atomic bonding environment by reducing the overall electronegativity difference and lattice rigidity, leading to improved dislocation mobility in the BCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: Replacing a fraction of Mo with Nb lowers the inherent brittleness due to Mo's high shear modulus, while Nb’s known role in enhancing fracture strain (as evidenced in similar RHEAs) ensures that solid solution strengthening is retained, thereby yielding improved ductility without a significant loss in strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The alloy’s room-temperature yield strength is expected to remain in the range of 1650–1719 MPa, while the compressive plastic strain improves from the baseline 12–27% to approximately 35% or higher, depending on the exact substitution level.
generation.baseline: The starting equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy exhibits a compressive yield strength of ~1719 MPa with limited plasticity at room temperature.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected to manifest under room-temperature compression in disordered BCC alloys; if too much Mo is replaced (beyond 30%), phase instability or significant strength loss may occur.
generation.uncertainty: While data indicate that increased Nb content can improve ductility, the precise optimum Nb/Mo ratio is uncertain. Direct experimental studies on Nb-substituted NbZrTiHfMo alloys are limited; if phase stability is compromised or the yield strength decreases by more than 15%, the hypothesis would be challenged.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of NbZrTiHfMo alloys with 10%, 20%, and 30% of Mo substituted by Nb. Evaluate the phase structure via XRD and SEM, and perform room-temperature compression tests to assess yield strength and fracture strain.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (phase identification, grain structure) via XRD and SEM/TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-substituted alloys exhibit a drop in yield strength exceeding 15% compared to the baseline or fail to improve ductility (i.e., fracture strain remains below ~35%), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure. These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C,. Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm3) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added. This resulted in RHEAs with lower densities and high-temperature strengths better than the properties of Ni-based superalloys and Fe-based steels. Comparing the performance at room temperature, HfMoTaTiZr alloy has the best yield strength 1600 MPa; HfMoNbTaTi has the highest 27% fracture strain; comprehensively, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical properties (yield strength 1369 MPa and 27% fracture strain). The fracture strain increases from 4% for the HfMoTaTiZr alloy to 12% for HfMoNbTaTiZr. The presence of Ta can increase the yield strength but decrease the toughness. Ti seems to have no significant influence on strength, but it has a negative effect on toughness. Zr increases the strength; however, it strongly deteriorates the toughness at room temperature, because the fracture strain decreases from 27% for the HfMoNbTaTi alloy to 12% for HfMoNbTaTiZr. The presence of Mo, which has the highest shear modulus, increases the yield strength at room temperature from 929 MPa to 1512 MPa significantly. Nevertheless, the toughness decreases tremendously, fracture strain declines from > 50% to 12%. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications.
